strengths: The paper presents an interesting and potentially useful set-level perspective: model multiplicity can provide alternatives after failures while exposing additional information when many models are disclosed. Connecting Rashomon sets, reactive robustness, stability, and privacy is conceptually original and relevant to ML governance.

The manuscript is generally well organized and clearly distinguishes reactive switching from ensemble robustness. It also appropriately notes that distributional leakage is not the same as membership leakage.

The empirical study covers six tabular datasets, uses exact/large sparse-tree Rashomon sets, reports five-fold or five-seed aggregation, and includes useful ablations over model-selection strategies. The appendix provides hyperparameters, computational resources, proofs, and additional plots.
Several mathematical results are valid, useful continuity or counting observations, notably the bounded-loss distribution-shift inclusion and neighboring-dataset Rashomon-set inclusion results.
weaknesses: The main privacy claims are not supported by the theory. Theorem 1 only bounds the entropy of a finite tree representation; low mutual information on average is not a formal privacy guarantee. More importantly, Theorem 6 bounds prediction KL divergence to p(x), not information about training examples. Its decreasing variance term does not establish that actual KL decreases monotonically, much less that releasing models leaks private data. The irreducible bias term (p(x)-mu(x))^2 can dominate. Thus the claimed theoretical robustness–privacy trade-off does not follow.

The manuscript incorrectly uses Theorem 5 to suggest membership privacy and alignment with differential privacy. Set inclusion after enlarging the Rashomon tolerance by 2K/n neither bounds distinguishability of a release mechanism nor says that an exact released model is similarly likely under neighboring datasets. No randomized mechanism or likelihood-ratio guarantee is defined. This is a material privacy and ethics overclaim.

The robustness argument has a formal inconsistency: H(f,f_hat) is defined using predictions on the clean inputs x_i, but Equation (1) replaces disagreement on attacked inputs x'_i by that quantity. Without an assumption connecting clean and attacked disagreement, the displayed equality and the ensuing interpretation are invalid. Moreover, the presented upper triangle bound alone does not force another model to inherit the attacked model's high loss; the needed lower bound is not stated.

The experiments establish only oracle robustness to a non-adaptive attack targeted at the original optimal tree: performance is the best accuracy among selected alternatives after seeing the adversarial dataset. They do not provide a deployable method for detecting the attack or choosing the replacement without adversarial labels, and do not test an adaptive attacker targeting the replacement or disclosed set. Consequently, the broad claims about reactive or moving-target robustness are substantially stronger than the evidence.

The empirical privacy evidence is narrow and only loosely connected to the theory: DRAFT reconstruction is evaluated on 100-point training subsets with up to 200 released trees, while the theory concerns KL of averaged probabilistic predictions and individual-tree mutual information. There is no membership-inference evaluation, no calibrated privacy measure, and no comparison to privacy-preserving baselines. The effects of model count, structural diversity, and the selection heuristic are not cleanly separated; indeed, the appendix reports that evenly spaced sampling leaks more than the nominally 'farthest' strategy.

The stability theorems are generic consequences of bounded-loss/total-variation inequalities and tolerance relaxation. They do not demonstrate stability at a fixed operational tolerance, and calling neighboring Rashomon sets 'indistinguishable' is misleading. The experiment also appears internally inconsistent when describing epsilon-prime as both epsilon and epsilon+2K/n.

Reproducibility is only partial: datasets, principal hyperparameters, hardware, and sampling schedules are described, but no code or artifact availability is stated, and important details of splits, preprocessing, DRAFT configuration, and model-selection tie breaking are incomplete. The absence of a focused limitations/ethics discussion is especially problematic given the policy recommendations, privacy language, oracle threat model, and use of sensitive lending and criminal-justice datasets.

strengths: The set-level perspective is interesting and potentially useful: the manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/dbe8bc9c72cc45ca96be44c1a4c87e96/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} connects model multiplicity to attack transferability, stability, and disclosure risk under one conceptual framework.

The empirical study covers six public tabular datasets, uses exact sparse-tree Rashomon sets, reports five-fold or five-seed aggregation, and explores several model-selection strategies. The appendix provides proofs, computational resources, and important experimental details.

Some formal components are sound within their limited scope, particularly the generic continuity/set-inclusion results in Theorems 4 and 5 and the finite-population variance calculation underlying Theorem 6.
The main narrative and figures are generally easy to follow, and the authors appropriately describe parts of the analysis as illustrative rather than exhaustive.
weaknesses: The central robustness argument is not technically supported. Equation (1) defines Hamming diversity on the original inputs x_i but its derivation requires disagreement on the adversarial inputs x'_i. Even with that correction, the displayed upper bound does not “force” two adversarial losses to be close, as claimed. The linear-model results establish a relative attack multiplier or an asymptotic ordering under strong assumptions, not that a more angular model has good absolute adversarial risk. The highly restricted rule-list theorem is likewise generalized far beyond its assumptions.

The empirical notion of reactive robustness is an oracle best-of-set metric: after attacking the optimal tree, the evaluation selects the tree with the highest accuracy on the labeled adversarial dataset. This maximum mechanically improves as candidates are added and does not give a deployable selection rule. An adaptive attacker aware of switching, attacks against the selected alternative, detection errors, and clean test performance after switching are not evaluated. Thus the experiments show limited transfer from one fixed target, not operational robustness.

The privacy theory conflates several distinct quantities. Theorem 6 bounds KL divergence between a conditional label distribution and an ensemble prediction; this is predictive approximation, not information about the training sample and hence not by itself privacy leakage. A decreasing upper bound does not prove that actual KL decreases, much less that training-data leakage increases. Moreover, the theorem assumes every base model predicts in [delta,1-delta], whereas the evaluated classification trees make hard 0/1 predictions. Theorem 1 is only a hypothesis-class entropy upper bound and does not establish that one learned sparse tree is more private than another; the asserted continuous linear-model analogue does not follow from the finite counting proof.

Theorem 5 provides inclusions only after relaxing the Rashomon tolerance. It neither makes the exact released sets indistinguishable nor yields differential privacy: deterministic outputs can reveal membership even when relaxed sets overlap. The manuscript's claims that this result protects membership privacy and aligns with differential privacy are therefore unsupported.

The reconstruction experiments do not bridge these theoretical gaps. DRAFT is applied to unusually small 100-record training sets, and giving it more trees supplies more constraints by construction. There is no comparison at fixed model count that cleanly separates diversity from other structural differences, no membership-inference evaluation, and no realistic disclosure threat model. The reported “trade-off” also combines reconstruction error with the oracle maximum adversarial accuracy, making both axes mechanically dependent on the number of released models.

Significance and originality are limited by these issues: the sound results largely specialize standard total-variation/Pinsker, neighboring-dataset, counting, and finite-sampling arguments, while the novel robustness–privacy conclusion is precisely the part not established by the theory or evaluation. The governance recommendations consequently overreach the evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete. There is no code or artifact statement, and important details such as exact data splits, preprocessing thresholds, random seeds, DRAFT configuration, attack/evaluation partitions, and model tie handling are missing. There are also inconsistencies such as describing an L-infinity attack with eta=0.1 after binary preprocessing in one experiment and a one-bit L0/L1 attack elsewhere, plus an incorrect “Number of Trees” x-axis label in Figure 14.

The paper lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion despite making recommendations for lending, recidivism, and healthcare governance. It does not discuss dataset bias, whether feature flips are semantically valid, harms from rotating to a differently behaving model, accountability and fairness implications, or risks of treating distribution approximation as personal-data leakage. These omissions are material because the policy claims depend on the threat model and deployment context.

strengths: The paper offers a timely and potentially useful conceptual perspective: treating the Rashomon set, rather than only a deployed model, as the object of robustness, privacy, and governance analysis. The empirical study covers six tabular datasets and very large enumerated sets of sparse trees. Figures 6–9 consistently show that trees farther from the attacked optimum tend to transfer attacks less, while releasing additional diverse trees improves dataset reconstruction.
The distribution- and dataset-shift inclusion results in Theorems 4 and 5 are simple but technically useful stability observations, and their assumptions are stated explicitly.

The manuscript is well organized and generally clear. Its distinction between reactive robustness, ensemble robustness, distributional leakage, and membership privacy is valuable, even though some later conclusions blur these distinctions.

The work has meaningful originality in connecting Rashomon-set diversity to a robustness–privacy tension and in exploring that connection using both sparse-tree enumeration and reconstruction attacks.
weaknesses: The central robustness argument contains a material mathematical error. Section 5.1 defines H(f,f_hat) using predictions on the original x_i, but Equation (1) replaces the needed disagreement on adversarial x'_i with this quantity. Moreover, the displayed upper bound L_S'(f) <= H + L_S'(f_hat) does not imply that small H forces the two losses to be close or that high H is required to outperform f_hat; a reverse-triangle lower bound using disagreement on S' would be needed. Thus the claimed general mechanism is not established as written.

The privacy theorem does not prove the claimed increase in leakage. Theorem 6 shows only that an upper bound on KL divergence decreases with ensemble size; a decreasing upper bound does not imply that the actual KL divergence decreases. Nor does better approximation of P(y|x) by an ensemble, by itself, establish leakage of training examples or sensitive features. The synthetic experiment illustrates selected cases but cannot repair this logical gap.

Several broader privacy claims are unsupported. Theorem 1 is merely a hypothesis-class entropy upper bound and does not show that actual mutual information decreases monotonically with sparsity; its stated O(l_f log d) form also omits an additive O(l_f) term and fails literally at d=1. More seriously, the near-inclusion of Rashomon sets on neighboring datasets in Theorem 5 does not imply differential privacy or limited membership-inference advantage, since it provides neither randomized-output probability ratios nor a bound for a specified release mechanism.

The empirical trade-off is partly built into the evaluation. Robustness is the oracle-best adversarial accuracy among all released trees, which naturally benefits from a larger search set, while reconstruction receives all released trees and naturally benefits from more constraints. The attacker targets only the original optimal tree and is not adapted after model switching. Consequently, the experiments do not establish robustness against an adaptive adversary or a deployable model-selection policy, and there are no matched baselines disentangling cardinality, diversity, and model complexity.

Theorem 2 supports 'inherent vulnerability' only under restrictive conditions: binary features, a specially structured rule list with q_1=0, label-informed per-example perturbations, and particular majority predictions. Corollary 2 additionally requires a strictly decreasing loss for its strict inequality, and very large attack strength can make all compared models unusable. These results do not justify the manuscript's broad claims about inherently interpretable or sparse models generally.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix supplies datasets, major TreeFARMS parameters, hardware, and high-level sampling procedures, but no code or artifact, exact preprocessing thresholds, complete train/validation protocol, attack/DRAFT configuration, or random seeds. Most reconstruction results use only 100 training records and five repetitions, limiting external validity and uncertainty assessment.

The paper lacks a dedicated limitations and ethics discussion. This matters because it draws policy implications from public high-stakes datasets such as COMPAS and credit data, while the proposed reactive switching could introduce inconsistent decisions across individuals or time. Dataset-specific social limitations, adaptive threat models, access assumptions, and risks from retaining large internal model collections should be addressed explicitly.

strengths: The paper identifies a useful and timely set-level perspective: model multiplicity can provide alternatives after a deployed model is compromised while creating additional disclosure risk. Connecting Rashomon sets, moving-target defenses, and privacy is conceptually interesting and potentially significant.

The manuscript combines several forms of evidence, including theoretical results for trees and linear models, experiments on six tabular datasets, small neural networks, and concept-bottleneck models. The supplementary material provides proofs, dataset descriptions, hyperparameters, computational resources, and additional attack experiments.

The distribution-shift results are mathematically clean: Theorem 5.4 follows from bounded-loss continuity and Pinsker's inequality, while Theorem 5.5 correctly establishes set inclusion after expanding the Rashomon tolerance by 2K/n.

The empirical tree results consistently show that models farther from the attacked model often have lower attack transferability, with especially strong correlations on COMPAS, credit, diabetes, and FICO. The reconstruction experiments also provide suggestive evidence that diverse collections can reveal more than similar collections of equal size.

The paper is generally well organized, clearly written, and candid about several limitations, including attack-dependent notions of diversity, the distinction between distributional and membership leakage, and the illustrative rather than prescriptive nature of its deployment threshold.
weaknesses: The central privacy theory does not establish the claimed leakage result. Theorem 5.6 only bounds how a random subset average approaches the full-set mean mu(x); its bound retains the unrestricted bias term (p(x)-mu(x))^2. Nothing proves that the Rashomon-set mean approximates the data distribution, that actual KL divergence decreases monotonically, or that this predictive approximation constitutes leakage about the training data. Moreover, the KL result assumes every model output lies in [delta,1-delta], whereas the main decision trees output 0 or 1, so that result does not apply to the principal model class without an unstated smoothing procedure.

Theorem 4.1 is a hypothesis-class entropy bound, not a meaningful privacy guarantee. It gives no differential-privacy or individual-record protection, and an O(l_f log d) upper bound does not by itself show that increasing sparsity monotonically reduces actual mutual information for trained models. The manuscript consequently overstates this as 'sparse models are private.' Its appeal to generalization and stability likewise does not establish privacy for the algorithms studied.

The robustness theory supports substantially weaker conclusions than claimed. Equation (2) says disagreement is necessary for a large difference in adversarial loss, but does not show that disagreement is sufficient or that a diverse Rashomon set contains a robust alternative. Theorem 4.2 concerns a restricted class of rule lists, uses a perturbation budget depending on rule position and length, and can have a vacuous lower bound; it does not establish the broad claim that individual sparse models are inherently fragile.

The main reactive-robustness metric is the accuracy of the best member after observing an adversarial dataset. This is effectively an oracle selection metric: deployment would require detecting the attack, obtaining reliable labels on attacked inputs, and identifying the best replacement before adaptation by the adversary. These requirements are not modeled. The multi-model study covers only ten trees using a naive attack, which is insufficient evidence against an attacker aware of the released set or rotation policy.

The experimental trade-off is partly built into the protocol. Adding models gives the defender more chances to maximize adversarial accuracy and gives DRAFT more model constraints, so both trends can occur independently of a specifically Rashomon-induced trade-off. Equal-size, complexity-matched controls, non-Rashomon model pools, alternative privacy attacks, adaptive robustness attacks, and statistical tests are needed. Reconstruction error over only 100 training records is also not automatically a membership-privacy measure, contrary to the claim that this attack is necessarily stronger than membership inference.

There are material inconsistencies and ambiguities in the attack setup. The tree robustness appendix reports an L-infinity budget of 0.1 after feature binarization, while other experiments use a one-bit L0 perturbation; the relationship between these threat models and whether generated inputs remain semantically valid is unclear. Clean-data Hamming distance is substituted for the attacked-input disagreement appearing in the bound, without a guarantee connecting them.

Reproducibility is incomplete. No code or artifact availability statement is given, and important details such as train/validation splits, preprocessing thresholds, optimization schedules for neural networks, AWP sampling details, exact DRAFT configuration, probability smoothing for KL, and the full operational-selection implementation are missing. Several Rashomon tolerances and regularizers are tuned to obtain convenient set sizes, which complicates comparison across datasets.

The stability results are correct but generic continuity observations, and expanding epsilon can make overlap nearly automatic; describing neighboring Rashomon sets as 'indistinguishable' and relating this to differential privacy is not justified because set inclusion does not control output probabilities or privacy loss.

The ethics discussion is too brief for the proposed high-stakes deployment setting. Rotating among disagreeing models can create inconsistent decisions, fairness changes, auditability problems, and strategic adaptation, while releasing models trained on COMPAS or credit data raises concrete privacy and governance concerns. These risks and the limitations of the proposed illustrative 35% privacy threshold need explicit treatment. Overall, the conceptual direction has merit, but unsupported central privacy and robustness claims currently prevent acceptance.

strengths: Originality/significance: Treating the Rashomon set itself as a governance object and jointly examining robustness, stability, and privacy is an interesting framing with potential practical relevance. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/543cec89afcc4660a5a5674616ba1322/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Soundness: Some supporting results are correct and clearly proved, including the bounded-loss stability inclusions in Theorems 5.4–5.5 and the finite-population variance calculation underlying Theorem 5.6.

Evaluation: The study covers six tabular datasets, several selection strategies, small neural networks, and pretrained concept-bottleneck models; it reports repeated trials or folds for many experiments.
Presentation: The manuscript is well organized, visually polished, and generally clear about the intended intuition behind reactive model switching.
Reproducibility: The appendix reports datasets, computational resources, many TreeFARMS parameters, attack budgets, model architectures, and sampling procedures.
weaknesses: Soundness—privacy: Theorem 5.6 does not establish that releasing more models increases leakage. It gives a decreasing upper bound on approximation error, but the actual error need not decrease, and the persistent bias term |p(x)-μ(x)| can be arbitrarily large. Approximating a population or empirical conditional distribution is also not, by itself, a recognized guarantee of training-record privacy.

Soundness—internal inconsistency: The KL part of Theorem 5.6 assumes every model output lies in [δ,1-δ], whereas the TreeFARMS classifiers used in the corresponding simulation produce hard 0/1 predictions. With nondegenerate p(x), the reported KL divergence can then be infinite. The manuscript does not explain the smoothing or clipping apparently needed to obtain Figure 5.

Soundness—privacy interpretation: Theorem 4.1 is only a hypothesis-class entropy bound. It does not provide differential privacy, reconstruction protection, or an individual-record guarantee, yet the paper repeatedly characterizes sparse trees as private. Likewise, small generalization gaps do not generally constitute membership privacy.

Soundness—robustness: Equation (2) says large disagreement is necessary for a large risk difference, not that disagreement yields robustness. Nevertheless, the text often treats diversity as sufficient. The ensemble results additionally assume independent or weakly correlated attack failures without showing that the paper's diversity measures imply those assumptions.

Evaluation—mechanical selection advantage: Reactive robustness is usually measured by attacking the optimal model and then reporting the best accuracy among an expanding pool. This statistic is mechanically nondecreasing with pool size and uses an oracle choice informed by performance on attacked, labeled examples. It does not demonstrate a deployable switching rule or robustness to an adaptive adversary.

Evaluation—weak attack model: Most tree experiments use attacks targeted at one disclosed model. The multi-model experiment is limited to ten trees, 100 training examples, and a described-as-naive joint search. The claim that multi-model attacks are computationally difficult is not established by systematic baselines, attack-strength controls, or adaptive threat-model analysis.

Evaluation—trade-off identification: Increasing the number of released trees simultaneously changes pool size, diversity, information exposed to DRAFT, and the opportunity to select an extreme robust model. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate a diversity-induced robustness–privacy trade-off. Relevant controls such as matched-size/matched-diversity collections and independently trained non-Rashomon models are missing.

Evaluation—conflicting evidence: The neural membership-inference results are explicitly nonmonotonic and based only on Iris, Seeds, and Wine, yet are presented as confirmation of the claimed privacy trade-off. The tree privacy study uses only 100 training records and one specialized reconstruction attack, limiting external validity.

Significance: The stability theorems are generic consequences of total-variation bounds or changing at most K samples, and require relaxing the Rashomon tolerance from ε to ε+2K/n. Calling the resulting sets “indistinguishable” or claiming that a set remains valid without recomputation materially overstates what the inclusions prove.

Reproducibility/presentation: No code or artifact link is provided, and several consequential details are missing, including exact preprocessing thresholds, data splits, how KL infinities are handled, and complete optimization/training settings for the neural experiments. Tuning ε to obtain at least 100,000 trees also makes comparisons data-dependent.

Limitations and ethics: The impact statement is generic, and there is no focused limitations discussion covering oracle model selection, adaptive attackers, access assumptions, or the distinction between distribution learning and personal-data leakage. The proposed operational rule uses an illustrative 35% privacy-loss threshold and calls it a safety constraint despite lacking a formal privacy guarantee; that framing is risky for the high-stakes applications invoked by the paper.

Overall: The set-level perspective and breadth are promising, but the central privacy claim and the causal interpretation of the robustness–privacy trade-off are not supported by the theory or experimental design. These are fundamental rather than presentational shortcomings, so substantial reformulation and new controlled evaluation would be required before acceptance.

strengths: The paper offers an original and useful set-level perspective on trustworthy ML: diversity among near-optimal models can reduce attack transferability while potentially increasing aggregate information exposure. This framing is conceptually interesting and relevant to model governance.

The presentation is clear and well organized. Definitions, main results, proofs, and experimental details are easy to locate, and the summary table usefully connects the different hypothesis spaces and trustworthiness criteria.

The empirical study is unusually broad: six tabular datasets, exhaustive sparse-tree Rashomon sets, synthetic validation, small neural networks, and concept-bottleneck image models. Reported resources, hyperparameters, dataset sizes, attacks, selection strategies, and repeated trials provide a reasonable basis for reproduction, although code availability is not stated.

The paper appropriately distinguishes reactive robustness from conventional single-model robustness and acknowledges that useful diversity must align with the attack geometry. The poor transferability observed among trees and concept-bottleneck models is promising evidence for this phenomenon.

The manuscript considers societal implications of releasing multiple models and offers an operational privacy-first selection proposal. It does not ignore the risks exposed by its own analysis, and there are no apparent unresolved research-ethics violations.
weaknesses: The central privacy interpretation is not technically established. Theorem 5.6 only shows that averaging more sampled predictions reduces a finite-sampling variance term around the Rashomon-set mean; a potentially large bias term between that mean and p(x) remains. Closeness to an empirical conditional distribution is neither mutual information about the dataset nor a formal privacy guarantee, so the theorem does not by itself demonstrate progressively increasing training-data leakage.

The assumptions of Theorem 5.6 are also mismatched with its stated binary-classification setting: hard tree predictions are 0 or 1, whereas the KL result assumes every model output lies in [delta,1-delta]. The empirical reconstruction experiment is suggestive, but it uses only 100 binarized training records and one specialized attack, and therefore does not repair the general theoretical claim.

The paper repeatedly equates limited information capacity, stability, and privacy too strongly. Theorem 4.1 is essentially a hypothesis-class counting bound and does not imply differential privacy or protection for particular individuals. Likewise, Theorem 5.5 gives set inclusions only after expanding the Rashomon tolerance by 2K/n; this does not make the released sets indistinguishable and does not support the claimed analogy to differential privacy or membership protection.

Reactive robustness is evaluated largely through an oracle-style protocol: attack one designated model and then report the best accuracy among available alternatives. A deployment needs a reliable way to identify which replacement is safe, generally without labels for attacked inputs. The claim that attack identification is unnecessary does not address this model-selection problem.

The robustness threat model is limited. Most results concern attacks optimized for one fixed model, while an adversary aware of model rotation or the disclosed set can attack the policy or multiple models adaptively. The appendix's multi-model experiment uses only 100 records, at most ten trees, and a naive exponential search whose apparent weakening as constraints are added is not convincing evidence against adaptive attacks.

Equation 2 establishes only that disagreement is necessary for a large loss difference; high disagreement is not sufficient for improved robustness. Several surrounding statements and governance recommendations read as stronger than this result supports.

The direct trade-off plots use best-of-set adversarial accuracy and model groups produced by evenly spaced resampling. These groups are not clearly nested, so changes attributed to releasing additional models can also arise from changing which models are selected. Using a maximum further guarantees an opportunity benefit as pool size grows and can exaggerate operational robustness.

Theorem 4.2's proof appears to require additional structural assumptions. The construction for moving a negative example to the first positive rule separately modifies features to satisfy that rule and to evade all earlier rules, but overlapping or contradictory literals can invalidate the stated l+I-1 construction; the special l=1 argument is particularly insufficiently justified.

The stability results are mathematically modest continuity/inclusion statements under very small shifts and relaxed tolerances. They guarantee only relative near-optimality, not acceptable absolute accuracy, so claims that a set can be reused without recomputation are stronger than the guarantees.

Overall, the work has a strong idea, good exposition, and substantial empirical effort, but several central privacy and deployment claims exceed what the theory and experiments demonstrate. Correcting the formal privacy interpretation and evaluating adaptive, operational model switching are necessary before the contribution can be relied upon.
